2 Abstract 36 The aim of this study was to analyze the trend in mortality from uterine neoplasms and 37 their risk factors, specified by the International Classification of Diseases - 10th Edition 38 (ICD-10): C53, C54 and C55. This is an ecological study of a cross-sectional cohort and 39 time series of deaths from uterine cancer that were recorded on the death certificates of 40 147 women residing in Maringá -PR from 2004 to 2014. Deaths attributed to malignant 41 neoplasms of the cervix, unspecified (C53.9) were the most common among these 42 women. There was an increasing trend in mortality rates from cancer of the uterus. The 43 behavior of age groups showed an increase in women over 65 years of age. Overall, 44 71.5% of the women had less than 8 years of education, and 60.5% had no partner. It 45 was also found that the health unit in Vardelina had the highest number of dea ths, 46 corresponding to 0.73% of the population. The percentage of the total deaths in the city 47 was 0.15%. These data indicate that women in lower social strata have less access to 48 health services and less information regarding primary prevention and the eff ective 49 treatment of uterine cancer. 50 51 Keywords: Mortality; Integral Assistance to Women's Health; Uterine neoplasms 52 53 Introduction 54 Cervical cancer neoplasms rank third among the most common cancers affecting 55 women, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) such as Brazil [1]. In the 56 Americas, mortality attributed to cervical cancer has been estimated to be 38,362 deaths 57 in 2015. Together with other uterine neoplasms, the number of deaths reached 52,215. 58 Morbidities were reported in an alarming number of women (88,492). In Brazil, the 59 incidence of cervical cancer was 18.20 per 100,000 women between the ages of 50 -65 60 years, and approximately 16,340 new cases were observed from 2016 [2]. 61 Despite this high incidence, uterine neoplasms consist of mal ignant cervical 62 neoplasms, malignant neoplasms of the uterus, and malignant uterine neoplasms of 63 unspecified origin [1]. Neoplasms of the uterus, specifically the endometrium, are the 64 sixth most common of all cancers [3]. The incidence is greater (5.5%) in high-income 65 countries (HIC) compared to low-income countries (LIC) (4.2%), although mortality due 66 to uterine neoplasms is higher in less developed countries. The cumulative risk of 67 endometrial cancer affecting women aged 75 is estimated to be 1.6% in high -income 68 countries and 0.7% in LIC [4]. Endometrial cancer is a neoplasm that primarily affects 69 perimenopausal and postmenopausal women, given that in nearly 90% of cases, 70 abnormal bleeding occurs in the early stages of the disease. The definitive diagnosis of 71

3 endometrial neoplasia is established through a histological examination of material 72 obtained through an endometrial biopsy, curettage, or hysteroscopy [5]. 73 The occurrence of uterine cancer is strongly associated with precarious social living 74 situations, low human development, absent or fragile community education infrastructure 75 and difficulties accessing public health services for the early diagnosis and treatment of 76 premalignant lesions [6]. Estimates made by the Economic Policy Department for the 77 concentration of income among the richest in Brazil point out that there is high inequality 78 at the top of income distribution, and it tends to limit equal opportunities in society, which 79 can inhibit economic growth. The richest 1% of the Brazilian population has 48.5% of the 80 income of the richest 5%. The level is comparable to that of Germany (49.4%) and the 81 United States (51.5%), which are the top developed countries when inequality is 82 measured in this way [7] 83 However, studies of data on mortality trends due t o uterine neoplasms that 84 address the cervix (C53), uterus (C54) and unspecified regions (C55) are currently 85 scarce. It is important to highlight that the effective detection of premalignant neoplasms 86 is related to a reduction in mortality and health care c osts, which may offer benefits to 87 population health and economic spheres that are useful in evaluating the cost -88 effectiveness of the preventative efforts of regular screening [8]. 89 Thus, the objective of this study was to analyze mortality trends due to ute rine 90 neoplasms and associated risk factors utilizing the criteria of the 10th revision of the 91 International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health problems (ICD -92 10): C53, C54, C55 in women in southern Brazil”. 93 Materials and Methods 94 Study Design and Setting 95 This was an ecological cross-sectional design incorporating time series methods 96 to study the mortality associated with uterine neoplasms, specifically, C53, C54, C55 of 97 the ICD-10, utilizing mortality records of female residents in the city of Maringá in Brazil 98 over a ten-year period from 2004-2014. 99

4 Maringá, a medium -sized city in Southern Brazil, has a population of 397,437 100 inhabitants, of whom 185,353 (46.64%) are female, and 98,625 (53.21% of females) are 101 older than 20 years. Maringá has a high level of human development (.808), the 23rd 102 highest of all Brazilian municipalities [9]. In relation to primary care services, the Family 103 Health Strategy uses 72 family health teams operating out of 32 health centers to reach 104 240,156 people, corresponding to a 67.3% coverage level. It is divided into 9 Nuclei for 105 the Support of Family Health (NSFH) and 556 census tracts [10]. 106 Data Sources 107 Cases of uterine neoplasm mortality were selected according to the ICD-10 from 108 secondary databases of epidemiological surveillance sectors of the Departments of the 109 Family Health Strategy Women’s Health Program (Figure S1). 110 Variables such as age group, marital status, education level, and ethnicity, which 111 were available from death certificates and associ ated with mortality due to uterine 112 neoplasms, were analyzed. 113 The age group was divided in decades and the marital status was classified in 114 women with partners for those death certificates indicating the women were married and 115 women without partners for those who were single, divorced or widowed. The education 116 level variable was divided in years of study according to Law 5692/71, which considers 117 primary education to be up to 8 years of school. The knowledge of the variable can aid 118 planning processes, management and assessment of public health and school policies. 119 Illiterate people require special approaches for the practices of health promotion, 120 protection and recovery[11]. 121 As for the ethnicity, we chose to classify as white and other, which is justified by 122 the human diversity in the degree of miscegenation, from individual to individual, from 123 class to class, from region to region”. Also, indicators for indigenous, yellow and black 124 people must be regarded cautiously since these groups are very small in some s tates 125 and regions in Brazil. In addition, the samples for the whites are more robust, offering a 126 greater guarantee for usage (Brazil, 2008). Additional variables, considered risk factors, 127 were not analyzed because they do not appear on death certificates. 128 The information on the family income was raised using the data provided by IBGE 129 (Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics) through Demographic Census. The 130

5 systematization of these indicators is in conformity with the international 131 recommendations and contributes for the understanding of how the demographic, social 132 and economic profiles of the population modify, thus, making it possible to monitor social 133 policies and to disseminate relevant information for Brazilian society. Additional 134 variables, considered risk factors, were not analyzed because they do not appear on 135 death certificates. 136 137 Figure S1. Selection of cases of uterine according to ICD-10. 138 139 Data Analysis 140 Coefficients of mortality (CM) for the primary cause of death were calculated 141 employing a numerator of the total deaths from uterine neoplasms and a denominator of 142 the total female population exposed to the risk multiplied by 100,000. Then, for greater 143 detail, CM calculations from uterine neoplasms were carried out by specific grouping and 144 for each age group, organized in ten-year increments. 145 The data were entered in spreadsheets using ExcelR 2010 for Windows for the 146 adequate storage of information. Statis tical analyses were conducted descriptively 147 through calculations of the mean, median, maximum and minimum values, standard 148 deviation, and absolute and relative frequencies (percentage), along with line graphs. 149 The inferential analyses employed with the int ention of confirming or refuting evidence 150 found in the descriptive analysis was the Pearson chi-square test. 151 For the trend analysis, a polynomial regression model was utilized in which CM 152 were considered the dependent variable (y), and years of schooling were the 153 independent variable (x). The variable “year” was transformed in a year -centered 154 variable (x-2009), and the series were smoothed through the moving average of three 155 points. 156 The linear, quadratic, and cubic polynomial regression models were tested. 157 However, after verification of the dispersion diagram, only the first -order (linear) 158

6 equations were retained for this study. The significance level was set at α <0.05 for all 159 models. For the selection of the best -fitting model, the dispersion diagram, value of the 160 coefficient of determination (R -squared) and analysis of the residuals (assumptions of 161 true homoscedasticity were considered. When all criteria were found to be significant for 162 multiple models and when the coefficients of determination were similar, simpler models 163 were selected. 164 A choropleth map was constructed to show the distribution of mortality 165 percentages by health center, overlaying the average population income by census tract 166 of the studied municipality using the open-source software QGIS version 2.8 (REF). The 167 socioeconomic income variable was obtained for each census tract through the website 168 of the city health department of Maringá [9]. The descriptive and inferential analyses 169 were conducted in Microsoft Excel (version 2013), Epi Info 2005 and SPSS, version 20.1. 170 The sig nificance level for all analyses was set at α <0.05. Information collected was 171 collected after approval for the Research Ethics Committee of the State University of 172 Maringá with protocol number 86.4889. 173 Results 174 Over the period studied, there were a total of 8.924 cases of mortality (44.3%) in 175 women due to neoplasms, 147 (1.65%) of which were specifically uterine neoplasms. 176 Among deaths from uterine neoplasms, 57.8% were malignant uterine neoplasms of 177 unspecified origin. 178 The mean age of these women was 62 years with a standard deviation of 15 years. In 179 relation to education level, 71.5% of women had completed less than 8 years of formal 180 education. 79.6% of women were white, and 60.5% of women did not have a partner. 181 The results were meaningful regarding the ethnic group for the three types of uterine 182 cancer; as for the marital status, there was significance for ICD C54 and C55, and only 183 for C54 regarding education level. (Table S1) 184 185

The study showed that the Vardelina and Grevílea health 211 centers possessed a lower mean household income and a greater mean number of 212 deaths, corresponding to 0.73% and 0.54% of the population, respectively, whereas the 213 mean percentage of deaths in the municipality was 0.15% 214 In figures S3A and S3B, it is evident that mortality from neoplasms of the cervix 215 (C53) occurs with greater frequency in the majority of health centers and that all 216 neoplasms are more prevalent in areas that have a less favorable value of mean 217 household income. 218 219

11 Discussion 225 Literature involving data on mortality trends in uterine neoplasms that distinguish 226 between the cervix (C53), uterus (C54), and uns pecified origin (C55) is lacking. 227 Therefore, the objective of this study was to present data on mortality trends due to these 228 neoplasms. Mortality attributed to unspecified cervical neoplasms (ICD-10, C53.9) most 229 frequently affected women. The tendency of the CM for uterine neoplasms rose with a 230 mean of 7.41 and an increase of 0.13 per year. There was a mean of 4.14 and an 231 increase of 0.12 per year for cervical neoplasms. 232 The behavior of age groups in the study revealed an increase in the number of 233 mortality cases in women 65 years or older. This result may reveal the deficiencies of 234 the public health system regarding young women actively going through preventive 235 examinations, since these neoplasms are silent and take a long time to reach the final 236 stage of the disease. Findings of the variable of education level indicated that a majority 237 of women had less than 8 years of formal schooling. Schooling is an indirect indicator of 238 the family’s socioeconomic status and a risk predictor of chronic disease. This factor may 239 be related to women not understanding the orientations made by professionals, as well 240 as the malignancy of this pathogenesis. G iven this hypothesis, we believe that this 241 variable may be indicative of improvements in the approach strategies in the guidelines. 242 There was a significant increase among white women in relation to marital status, 243 with a majority of deaths occurring in women without partners. This piece of information 244 may indicate the likely multiplicity of partners, thus being exposed to sexually transmitted 245 diseases, increasing the risk for uterine neoplasms. 246 The distribution of deaths by location revealed that the Vardelina health center 247 experienced the greatest amount of deaths over the studied period, with a percentage 248 higher than the municipalities, suggesting also that the percentage of deaths was greater 249 in health centers closer to census tracts with a lower mean household income. 250 In figures S3A and S3B, it is evident that mortality from neoplasms of the cervix 251 (C53) occurs with greater frequency in the majority of health centers and that all 252 neoplasms are more prevalent in areas that have a less favorable valu e of mean 253 household income. The debate over inequality in income distribution has grown in recent 254 years. In a global perspective, Latin American countries in general, and particularly 255 Brazil, stand out for this inequality, which tends to limit equal opportunities in society and 256 may be an inhibitor of socioeconomic growth [12]. Since one of the risk factors related 257 mainly to cervical cancer is socioeconomic conditions, the research is in line with 258 perspectives related to the economy and health of women in less favored regions. 259

12 If, on one hand, assistance technologies have decisively influenced results in the 260 area, with significant advances; on the other hand, they accentuate inequalities in 261 societies where access to this type of assistance is not guaranteed for the whole 262 population, as is the case of Brazil. Small differences in the access to secondary 263 (specialties) and tertiary (treatment) services, which are highly effective, can result in 264 large differences in mortality. 265 Previous studies of non-Hispanic white women have indicated that in 2008, only 266 three types of cancer were responsible for 10% of mortality related to neoplasms overall. 267 It was observed that approximately 460,000 women died from breast cancer, 140,000 268 women died from ovarian cancer, and 74 ,000 women died from endometrial cancer, 269 which was found to be the most common among uterine neoplasms [13]. In the Republic 270 of Korea, the mortality incidence per 100,000 women decreased from 12.7 in 2000 to 271 11.8 in 2008. However, the age group of 25 -29 years experienced an elevated rate in 272 2011 (6.5) than when compared to 2000 (3.6) [14]. 273 Studies carried out in Kanagawa and Japan show that cervical cancer mortality 274 trends are rising in the 20 -29-year and 30 -39-year age groups, revealing concern for 275 cervical cancer among Japanese women younger than 50 years [15]. 276 A study of cervical cancer mortality in health regions of the Brazilian state of 277 Pernambuco observed a greater number of cases among non -white women. Women 278 who lacked formal schooling altogether and those with lower education levels (1-3 years 279 of schooling) were at an increased risk of death due to the disease, a fact that was found 280 to be independent of race. It was also found that a greater number of deaths from these 281 cancers occurred in unpartnered women compared to married women [16]. 282 Various interactions between health systems and individual -level factors over 283 time likely contributed to the rates observed in the city of Maringá. Diverse changes in 284 Brazilian health policy and other national, state, and municipal initiatives, particularly with 285 respect to women’s health, helped to design and implement strategies for the early 286 detection of uterine neoplasms. Such policy changes may have contributed to 287 improvement in the monitoring of indicators related to women’s health. However, it would 288 be beneficial if there were continued improvement in the monitoring of data on the 289 capacity of health professionals in relation to early detection and treatment and tracking 290 efforts of uterine neoplasms, which would result in a reduction of coefficients. The data 291 presented here do not correspond to this expectation. Thus, the mortality rate would 292 likely be higher due to better registry infrastructure. However, the variability among years 293 across diverse areas of the city did not conform to this expectation. 294

13 The Family Health Strategy has become essential for providing information 295 pertinent to examinations and performing outreach via community health workers to 296 residences, as well as controlling the frequency with which women complete annual 297 examinations. The participation of the entire health team, including members from both 298 the Family Health Strategy and Nucleus for the Support of Family Health, is critical to 299 attracting women. 300 One potential limitation of this study was the utilization of secondary data, which 301 may be biased from underreporting of mortality due to uterine neoplasms. As estimating 302 depends closely on mortality information, the better the quality of information on mortality 303 is, the better the estimated information is. Since 2005, there has been an improvement 304 in the information on mortality in Brazil, reflected by the quality of the information 305 obtained from the basic cause of death in the death certificate. The current picture, 306 however, still shows some degree of underreporting and high percentage of classification 307 as "ill -defined causes" in some Federal Units. The estimates presented here are, 308 therefore, reflections of this scenario. Another factor to be considered is the progressive 309 and constant search f or the improvement of the quality of information, resulting, year 310 after year, in increased validity and accuracy of the annual estimates. Although there are 311 limitations, the estimates are believed to be capable of describing current patterns of 312 cancer deaths, making it possible to assess the magnitude and impact of this disease in 313 Brazil [3]. 314 Our findings carry implications that support the notion that health efforts should 315 be reconsidered and reformulated, considering greater planning and monitoring 316 strategies. In this context, we emphasize the importance that the issues examined in this 317 study hold for healthcare professionals and stewards alike. These groups need to be 318 capable of identifying risk factors in women and subsequently offering adequate care 319 and coordination to reduce mortality indicators. 320 Studies that attempt to demonstrate the interrelationship among the SIAB, The 321 Cervical Cancer Information System, and The Family Health Strategy Laboratory System 322 are fundamental to understanding and mapping out specific efforts and program 323 strategies. Research that seeks to associate cervical cancer risk factors and strategies 324 that improve examination coverage are crucial for the reduction of mortality indicators. 325 Conclusion 326 This study identified a high number of deaths from uterine neoplasms, primarily 327 uterine neoplasms of an unspecified origin. In doing so, this study also showed that 328 mortality due to uterine neoplasms is increasing annually over the study period, mainly 329

14 in women who were 65 years or older, had lower education levels, and had low incomes, 330 which confirms past research in Brazil. 331 These data indicate that those in disadvantaged social strata are those with lower 332 access to health services and a diminished qualit y of information surrounding primary 333 prevention and the effective treatment of uterine neoplasms. 334 Our findings carry implications that support the notion that health efforts should 335 be reconsidered and reformulated, taking greater planning and monitoring strategies into 336 account. In this context, we emphasize the importance that the issue approached in this 337 study holds for healthcare professionals and stewards alike. These groups need to be 338 capable to identify risk factors in women and subsequently offer ade quate care and 339 coordination in order to reduce mortality indicators. 340 References 341 [1] Topan A, Ozturk O, Eroglu H, Hulya, Harma M I.
